argument: Steve presents Hegel's argument that popular ideas about God rest on unexamined assumptions, starting with the observation that words like 'God' never transmit an identical mental image between people, and that the common fundamentalist-vs-New-Atheist framing is a false dichotomy that hides centuries of other positions. Hegel argues God cannot be a 'being' at all, since to be a being in a universe of beings is to be finite, so instead he proposes God is the process of self-determination imbued into the cosmos, which connects to Hegel's earlier claim that self-knowledge makes you more fully real. Steve argues this reframing isn't a cheap trick but a genuine third option that appeals to both the science-minded skeptic and the spiritually inclined, and that refusing to engage with the word 'God' (or 'faith') at all just cedes those words to your opponent's cause.
keyIdeas: Common nouns like 'microphone' don't transmit an identical mental image between people, and 'God' works the same way -- each person's definition is an acquired assumption worth questioning before evaluating any argument about God.
The popular picture of belief as a line between religious fundamentalists and New Atheists is a false dichotomy that ignores the long history of other positions on God.

Hegel argues God cannot be a 'being' like an omniscient, omnipotent person, because to be a being in a universe made of beings is to be finite and limited, while God, if it exists, must be unlimited and infinite.

Hegel proposes instead that God is the process of self-determination imbued into the cosmos; since something that determines itself is more fully real than something dependent on outside forces, God becomes what is 'most fully real,' and humans approach that reality whenever they act from self-knowledge rather than outside conditioning.

Faith is better defined as belief without sufficient evidence rather than belief without any evidence at all, which matters because every belief, including the skeptic's, ultimately rests on some leap of faith -- so refusing to engage with the words 'faith' or 'God' just hands their merits to whoever else is using them.

terms.def: Steve's objection to framing belief about God as only two options (fundamentalism or New Atheism), which ignores the many other historical positions.
Something finite and limited by virtue of existing among other beings in the universe; Hegel argues God cannot be a being in this sense.
Hegel's proposed definition of God: the process by which something determines itself rather than being controlled by outside forces.
Belief without sufficient evidence (not belief without any evidence), a definition Steve argues applies to every belief, including the skeptic's.
